title: The US AI Labs, Part 2: The Suppliers Are Financing Their Own Customers
content:
This is Part 2 of a three-part series. Part 1 maps the nine US AI labs, what they earn and
what investors pay for that revenue. This part picks up where it ends.
Market Structure Brief · Part 2 of 3 • By codingplans.dev • Dataset verified 2026-10-27
The US AI Labs, Part 2: The Suppliers Are Financing Their Own Customers
In September 2025 NVIDIA offered OpenAI up to $100 billion to spend on NVIDIA systems. Five months later the offer had become $30 billion of ordinary equity, and the money was still expected to come back as chip orders. Across the labs, the suppliers' stakes are small next to the orders promised back, which leaves them holding the position Lucent held in 2000: an order book worth what the customer can pay.

On September 22, 2025, NVIDIA and OpenAI signed a letter of intent. NVIDIA would invest up to $100 billion in stages as OpenAI brought new data-centre capacity online, and OpenAI would fill that capacity with NVIDIA systems. The first $10 billion was to arrive once the two companies signed a definitive agreement for the purchase.
That agreement was never signed. By February 20, 2026, Reuters reported, it had taken much longer than either side expected, and NVIDIA was instead close to putting $30 billion into OpenAI's next funding round as an ordinary investor. The same source said OpenAI would spend much of the new money on NVIDIA chips. The round closed at the end of March at $122 billion, valuing OpenAI at $852 billion once the money was in.
The paperwork changed. The direction of the money did not.
Part 1 ended on the point that the suppliers are paid first. This part measures what they paid to get there and what they now hold. The filings show stakes that are small next to the orders that come back, so what the suppliers mostly own is a claim on the labs' ability to keep paying. Lucent owned the same kind of claim in 2000, and one difference decides most of the comparison.
Two thirds of OpenAI's round came from its suppliers
NVIDIA was not the largest supplier in that round. Amazon committed $50 billion, $35 billion of it conditional, and in the same announcement OpenAI expanded its AWS contract by $100 billion over eight years. Counting both commitments in full, the two companies that sell OpenAI its computing supplied $80 billion of the $122 billion.
SoftBank and the venture funds made up the rest. They have nothing to sell OpenAI, and they set the price alongside the suppliers. Still, most of the cash behind the $852 billion mark came from companies that expect much of it back as revenue.
Each dollar of supplier equity buys up to $22 of orders
OpenAI's terms are mostly reported. Anthropic's are filed, which makes it the better place to measure what a supplier's dollar buys. Its S-1 lists the stock each supplier agreed to buy this year and the spending Anthropic committed in return, and the table below puts them side by side. Amazon's terms are the steepest. In April it agreed to buy about $5 billion of Anthropic preferred stock, and in the same month Anthropic committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over ten years, "regardless of actual usage."
Anthropic promised $22 of orders for each dollar Amazon put in. Google's figure is about 11. AMD's is the only one in the filing written as a direct swap: AMD will buy up to $5 billion of Anthropic stock, drawable only as its GPUs are delivered and deployed, against hardware Anthropic expects to cost more than $20 billion.
At those ratios the equity works as a discount on the sale, paid in shares instead of price.
What the suppliers put in, and what comes back
Filed or announced terms · checked 2026-10-27
The ratio is shown only where both sides are stated in dollars. Amazon's $50 billion into OpenAI is set against the contract expansion announced with it, not OpenAI's total AWS spend.
One arrangement in the filing is a different instrument. In March Anthropic signed an equipment lease with Broadcom for specialised AI accelerators, and alongside it an agreement to issue up to $42 billion of convertible notes, to Broadcom or a financial partner, to pay for that lease. Anthropic describes the notes as available if needed. Here the supplier is not buying stock. It is lending the customer the money for the customer's own purchase, which is vendor financing in the textbook sense and the instrument Lucent used.
The risk has moved from the buyer's cash to the price of a token
At the end of 2000 Lucent had committed about $7.3 billion of credit to its own customers, including a $1.6 billion loan it was still finalising, and had guaranteed another $1.8 billion of their debt. Its quarterly filing explained how those sales were booked. Lucent counted the revenue when the customer's notes were "reasonably assured of collection," judged partly on whether Lucent could sell the notes on.
In December, three months after its fiscal year closed, Lucent cut $679 million from that year's revenue, which Time described as on-credit purchases that fell through. In January it reported quarterly sales down 28 percent and took a $1.6 billion restructuring charge. By February the SEC was looking at how it booked sales. The buyers Lucent had lent to were, in Time's phrase, start-ups and emerging companies, and when their funding dried up the loans and the sales went together.
Anthropic is not that customer. It brought in $16.29 billion of revenue in the first half of 2026, ended June with $131.65 billion in cash and short-term investments, and lost $693 million at the operating line. Nothing in the filing points to a collection problem today.
Further out, the comparison holds. The S-1 says Anthropic's compute commitments generally have to be paid whatever its revenue or utilisation, and the longest run to 2045. Its three cloud contracts alone, with Amazon, Google and Microsoft, total $269.4 billion. Spread evenly over their terms they come to about $33 billion a year, roughly 71 percent of the run-rate Anthropic cited in May. The contracts are priced in capacity and dollars, not tokens, so if the price of a token falls faster than usage grows, the same capacity earns less against the same bill.
A take-or-pay contract leaves the lab carrying the price of its own product, and the supplier carries it only if the lab can no longer pay.
The first disclosure to watch is a drawdown on the Broadcom notes, which would mean Anthropic is paying for hardware with its supplier's credit rather than its own cash. A supplier commitment rewritten the way NVIDIA's was in February would mean another link proved too hard to keep. The clearest signal would be a true-up payment, a lab paying for compute it did not use, because it would show usage falling behind the contracts.
If, on the other hand, committed spend shrinks as a share of revenue quarter after quarter, the labs are outgrowing their contracts, and the shares the suppliers took in place of a discount will be worth more than the discount was.
Until one or the other shows up, the suppliers hold what Lucent held: a book of orders whose value depends on the buyer. This buyer is far stronger, and the book is far larger. Lucent's customer credit came to $7.3 billion; Anthropic's three cloud contracts come to $269.4 billion.
Part 3 turns to the commodity itself. What a $500 billion annual token market would require, and what a
boken, one billion tokens, buys at today's prices.

report.summary: Chipmakers and cloud providers funded two-thirds of OpenAI's $122B round, and now hold order books worth only what the labs can keep paying.
report.background: AI labs now raise capital from the same companies that sell them compute. As training and inference costs outrun revenue, the money has increasingly looped: a supplier invests, the lab spends it back on that supplier's chips or cloud capacity, and both book the result as growth. The pattern echoes the telecom equipment vendor financing that unravelled around Lucent in 2000, when loans to start-up customers were counted as revenue until the customers' funding dried up. The difference now is scale and counterparty quality: Anthropic alone carries $269.4B of cloud commitments running to 2045 and ended June 2026 with $131.65B in cash, while OpenAI was valued at $852B on $122B of new capital. The structure converts supplier equity into a discount paid in shares, and pushes the real risk onto the price of a token rather than the buyer's balance sheet.
key_points: NVIDIA's September 2025 letter of intent to invest up to $100B in stages, tied to OpenAI filling new data centres with NVIDIA systems, never became a definitive agreement. By February 2026 it had been rewritten as roughly $30B of ordinary equity in OpenAI's next round, with the money still expected to return as chip purchases.

Suppliers supplied $80B of OpenAI's $122B round: Amazon committed $50B ($35B conditional) and simultaneously expanded its AWS contract by $100B. Counting both, two thirds of the capital behind the $852B valuation came from vendors, not from SoftBank or venture funds.

Anthropic's S-1 makes the exchange rate explicit. Amazon's ~$5B preferred stock purchase sits against a $110B ten-year spend commitment 'regardless of actual usage' — about $22 of orders per dollar invested. Google's ratio is around 11x; AMD's is a direct swap of up to $5B in stock against hardware drawing only as GPUs ship.

The Broadcom arrangement is textbook vendor financing: a $42B convertible note facility that Anthropic may draw to pay for an accelerator lease. Rather than buying equity, the supplier lends the customer the money for the customer's own purchase — the instrument Lucent used in 2000.

The risk has migrated to token pricing. Anthropic's three cloud contracts total $269.4B, roughly $33B a year, about 71 percent of its May run-rate. Take-or-pay terms price capacity in dollars, so if token prices fall faster than usage grows, the same bill buys less revenue.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this locks in an oligopoly: the labs that can sign decade-long take-or-pay contracts get capacity, and everyone else queues. It also flatters reported revenue on both sides of the deal, since a supplier's investment returns as its own top line — a circularity that makes growth metrics harder to read. For developers, the practical effect is durable but rigidly priced compute from three clouds and a handful of chip vendors, with less room for smaller providers. For regular users, cheap tokens are the goal but also the exposure: if prices fall faster than usage grows, labs carry the gap and must recover it through pricing, throttling or consolidation.
report.tools: To follow the story yourself: SEC EDGAR full-text search for S-1 and 10-Q filings (Anthropic's commitments and Lucent's 2000 disclosures are both there), OpenRouter and Artificial Analysis for live token-price and model benchmarks, Epoch AI for compute and cost trend datasets, and SemiAnalysis for supply-chain reporting. Crunchbase or PitchBook round data helps track which suppliers appear in which cap table.
